title: Wall Street Braces for Fed Rate Hold, but Rate Hike Talk Grows Louder
excerpt: All 104 economists in a Reuters poll expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates at its July 28-29 meeting, but a growing majority now sees the probability of a rate increase this year as high.
body:
Fed Expected to Stand Pat Next Week

The Federal Reserve is all but certain to leave interest rates unchanged when its policy committee meets July 28-29, according to a Reuters poll of 104 economists conducted between July 17 and 21. Every single forecaster expects the central bank to hold the federal-funds rate at 3.50% to 3.75%, and prediction markets echo that conviction — Polymarket is pricing a hold at 96%, while CME's FedWatch tool puts the probability at roughly 90%.

But behind that near-unanimous consensus on the July outcome, a sharp and uncomfortable shift is underway. Most economists who answered a separate question about the chances of a rate hike this year now describe the likelihood as "high." Last month, a majority had called it "low."

"If you're really serious about a return to 2% inflation then the time for hiking rates is kind of approaching."

— Jan Groen, Chief U.S. Economist, Société Générale

Five Years of Inflation, No Resolution

The Fed has now held rates steady four times in 2026 after three consecutive cuts in the second half of 2025. Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took the helm this year, has adopted a consistently hawkish posture, repeatedly framing the central bank's mandate in blunt terms: prices are too high, and the fight is not finished.

The numbers support his urgency. The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — stood at 4.1% in May, more than double the 2% target. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy, registered 3.4%. While June CPI data offered some relief — headline inflation dropped to 3.5% from 4.2% in May, and core CPI eased to 2.6% — the improvement may prove fragile.

A near-25% surge in oil prices following the collapse of the U.S.-Iran interim peace deal and renewed tensions near the Strait of Hormuz has pushed crude back above $75 a barrel. Markets are already pricing in two rate increases by end-March 2027 as a hedge against energy-driven inflation reigniting.

Bank of America Flips to Expecting Hikes

The most dramatic Wall Street reversal has come from Bank of America. Six months ago, the bank's economists expected rate cuts. Now, CEO Brian Moynihan says, "our belief is we'll raise rates."

In a CBS News interview, Moynihan warned that inflation would remain sticky enough to force the Fed's hand. "It's drifting down, and it's drifting down slower than people would like it," he said, pointing to persistent pressure from housing, food, and fuel costs. BofA now forecasts three quarter-point hikes — in September, October, and December 2026 — totaling 0.75 percentage points. That would lift the target range to 4.25%-4.50%.

Not everyone agrees. Nomura's senior U.S. economist Jeremy Schwartz sees Chairman Warsh as "more playing for time" rather than actively pushing toward tightening. "We see a lot of the areas Warsh is focusing on seem like the types of things you'd be talking about if you were building the case to stay on hold," Schwartz told Reuters.

A Divided Committee, a Delicate Balance

The June dot plot revealed a sharply divided Federal Open Market Committee. The median participant implied one quarter-point increase before year-end, and six of 18 members penciled in at least two. Governor Christopher Waller has publicly stated that policymakers may need to raise rates if underlying inflation continues to signal broad price pressure.

Among the 104 economists polled, 78 — a three-quarters majority — still see no rate change through the end of 2026. But among those who do expect a move, the balance has shifted decisively: most now project at least one rate increase, while only six still anticipate cuts.

JPMorgan economists noted that Warsh's newly established task forces — on communications, the balance sheet, and inflation — could reshape policy over the medium term. "The inflation task force could have the most lasting impact on the conduct of monetary policy," they wrote.

What It Means for NRI Investors and the Diaspora

For Indian-Americans and NRIs with dollar-denominated assets, the calculus is shifting. A higher-for-longer rate environment — or potential hikes — keeps U.S. mortgage rates elevated; the 30-year fixed rate has remained above 6% and recently touched an 11-month high of 6.62%. Savings accounts and CDs continue to offer attractive yields, but variable-rate debt becomes more expensive with each potential increase.

The interest-rate trajectory also has implications for the rupee. Sustained U.S. rates above 3.5% widen the dollar-rupee carry trade, putting downward pressure on the Indian currency and making remittances more valuable in rupee terms, while raising the cost of dollar-denominated education loans.

What to Watch at the July Meeting

The rate decision itself is a foregone conclusion. The real signals will come from the statement language — any hardening of inflation-risk framing would be read as teeing up a September move. Hawkish dissents in favor of a hike would matter more than the headline decision. And Warsh's press conference will be parsed for whether he leaves a September increase firmly on the table.

The wild card remains oil. If crude prices continue climbing on Strait of Hormuz escalation, the carefully constructed consensus around a hold could crack — and the Fed's next move may not be the one markets are hoping for.
